rows: COSHH requires adequate control of exposure to workplace materials that can cause ill health.
Hazardous substances may include dusts, gases, fumes, liquids, powders and harmful micro-organisms.
Employers should identify tasks involving hazardous substances and how harm could occur.
Prevention at source and substitution with safer substances or processes should be considered first.
Where prevention is not possible, exposure must be adequately controlled.
Control measures may include enclosure, local exhaust ventilation, procedures, supervision and respiratory protection.
Controls must be maintained, examined and tested as required.
COSHH assessments should be reviewed when circumstances change or controls may no longer be effective.
COSHH controls concern specific substances, processes and dutyholders and cannot be inferred from a property address alone.
Asbestos, lead and some other hazards have separate regulatory regimes and should not be treated as ordinary COSHH cases.
UKHSA and the Met Office operate Cold-Health Alerts for England.
Alerts are issued when forecast cold weather could have significant health impacts.
The core alerting period runs from 1 November to 31 March, with exceptional alerts possible outside it.
Alert levels use yellow, amber and red categories based on likely impact and likelihood.
Health and social care providers are given suggested preparedness and response actions.
Guidance prioritises people at greater risk from cold-related harm.
Providers should use alert action cards to align preparation and escalation.
Cold-health planning includes continuity, communication and support for vulnerable people.
An alert is a regional health-risk signal and not evidence of conditions inside a specific building.
Alert status changes with forecasts and must be checked against the current UKHSA service before operational use.
Meningococcal disease is uncommon but can cause meningitis or sepsis and can become severe rapidly.
Urgent medical assessment is required when meningitis or sepsis is suspected.
A rash may be absent, so response should not wait for a rash to appear.
UKHSA guidance covers diagnosis, surveillance, prevention, vaccination and treatment.
Public-health management includes actions after individual cases and clusters.
Chemoprophylaxis and vaccination decisions are based on exposure and public-health assessment.
Vaccination programmes target ages and groups at increased risk.
Health-protection teams coordinate case and cluster management.
General disease guidance does not demonstrate infection risk at a specific premises or parcel.
Outbreak advice, eligible groups and public-health actions can change and require current UKHSA confirmation.
Registered medical practitioners have statutory notification duties for specified infectious diseases.
Some diseases or situations require urgent notification to the local UKHSA health protection team.
Urgency may depend on outbreak context, rarity, ease of spread or patient risk.
Notification supports surveillance and public-health response.
Laboratories also have reporting duties for specified causative agents.
Reports should contain sufficient clinical and contact information for health protection action.
Suspected cases may be notifiable before laboratory confirmation where the legal criteria are met.
Health protection teams advise when reporters are uncertain about urgency.
Notification lists and urgency rules are clinical and public-health controls, not parcel risk scores.
Local case information is sensitive and should not be inferred or exposed without an authorised data source.
